summary:
Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but national legislation now restricts trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. Puno, as a Peruvian department, is bound by all of these measures: they are national in scope and the sources record no Puno-specific application, exemption or enforcement practice.

The operative restriction is the April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents. Its article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', with narrow exceptions for situations involving medical attention, custody, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities. The same package bans inclusive restroom signage such as 'women in their diversity' and, according to the Inter-American Advisory Opinion record, determines restroom entry by sex assigned at birth, which reaches trans youth as well as adults.

The legislative sequence is documented. On 20 February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante of Honor y Democracia; the measure stood at committee stage at that date. On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved the bill and exempted it from a second vote, after which it entered into force as national law. The stated trigger for the original bills was a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chávez airport.

Enforcement is expected to rest on the personal judgment of security staff, including checks of identity documents, which LGBTI activist Gianna Camacho identified as the practical consequence of the rule. Legal gender recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive, so a trans visitor's documents frequently do not correspond to presentation, and restroom access becomes the point at which that mismatch is tested. The policy has already reached private premises: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced it.

Hostility is not confined to signage and access. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'. On the floor of Congress, congressman Lizarzaburu made dehumanising comparisons about trans people, as recorded by the human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru.

Violence against trans people is documented and, by the account of report co-author Gianna Camacho, substantially under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and stressed that published figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law, so a bias-motivated assault against a trans visitor falls outside the hate-crime aggravation that other regional systems provide.

The constitutional framework points the other way. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. IDEHPUCP, in an analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of 15 April 2025, argues that the restroom provision breaches the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, that its aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, and that UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

Speech and association are constrained as well. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings, and in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.
tangentialFactors:
The bathroom restriction has no evidentiary base in the sources: Gianna Camacho notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms, while the law's justification rests on preventing child sexual abuse, a rationale IDEHPUCP identifies as a stereotype rather than a documented risk.

Peru's position is regionally unusual. After the 2017 repeal it stands with Paraguay and Guyana as the only South American states without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law, so visitors comparing protections across the continent will find a markedly thinner framework here.

Regional jurisprudence runs against the domestic restriction. Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 frames gender identity as protected personal autonomy, and the Azul Rojas Marín judgment is recorded as the Inter-American Court's first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reached through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

The removal of LGBT provisions from the Penal Code followed an April Constitutional Committee vote in 2017 and a petition claiming one million signatures, carried by Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members; the sequence indicates organised legislative opposition rather than an administrative omission.

Document checks are the likely flashpoint for a visitor: the same 2024-2025 measures pair a biological-sex test for facility use with identity documents that, because recognition is long and invasive, frequently do not match presentation.
localsOnly:
Residents face the same national restroom rule, but the practical burden lands on staff at gyms, malls, clinics and workplaces: a consumer-protection body has already dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, leaving individuals without an administrative remedy.

Inclusive signage is prohibited, which affects businesses, community organisations and events that display wording such as 'women in their diversity'; article 4 of the April 2025 law additionally bans media and advertising content under vague child-protection terms, and the minimum obscenity sentence rose from three to four years.

Peru's health authorities removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance in June 2024, a change directed at how trans patients are treated in healthcare settings and one that residents can invoke in clinical encounters.

Activist litigation remains available: a Lima constitutional court ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional in July 2025 after an activist legal challenge, and IDEHPUCP continues to publish constitutional analysis of the restroom provision.

Legal gender recognition remains long, costly and invasive, so mismatched documents persist in daily life for residents as well as visitors.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory records how the restroom restriction is applied in Puno specifically: which facilities check documents, whether any local authority or establishment has issued guidance, and whether complaints have been filed there are all unsourced. IDEHPUCP's April 2025 analysis addresses the national framework and records no Puno-specific finding.

The sources do not establish whether the ban on inclusive signage has been enforced against any premises, nor the penalty structure for breaching it.

Whether the 2017 hate-crime repeal affects charging decisions in individual assaults is asserted as a coverage gap only; no prosecution statistics for bias-motivated violence against trans people are given.

The July 2025 constitutional ruling is reported as invalidating an anti-equality decree, but the decree's content and whether it affected trans people's rights are not sourced here.

The claim that identity documents frequently do not match a trans person's presentation rests on the general description of recognition as long, costly and invasive; the inventory provides no statistics on recognition rates or processing times.

Enforcement expectations rest on Gianna Camacho's warning about security staff judgment and ID checks; whether this actually occurs at any given checkpoint is not documented.
